utterances.text: The check-point in Velagici was not the result of this order but part of the assessment of the security situation in the territory of the municipality. That also included the check-point near Ropac and the check-point at the entrance to Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: These check-points were also manned by men of various ethnicities; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these already were not because the war had broken out on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I am talking about the time before the 27th?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it was a misunderstanding, up to the 27th there was just this one check-point, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. We have evidence about that so I will not ask you anything else about this. Please tell me what was the function of the check-points in 1991, just in a few sentences like I asked you to do with one of your previous answers?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the dispatch following the action Check-Point specified what were the reasons for setting up the check-points, mainly it was checking the IDs of unidentified and suspect persons, the movements of military and para-military units, seizing weapons carried in public traffic but illegally, also monitoring the flow of goods because there was a shortage of certain goods, and also regular control because there was less -- and there were fewer mobile patrols and traffic controls.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I forgot to alert you but there's no reason for us to remain in private session unless we are already in public session. We can move to the public session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We are in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are, I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that this purpose of the check-points, or rather, the task of the men manning the check-points did not change from 1991 to 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically as far as the civilian police are concerned, it did not change, but when military hostilities broke out, the military police joined the check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. You explained everything else concerning the check-points, so I will move on. About the change of insignia on the uniforms that you spoke about, you will agree with me that the attempt to remove the five-pointed star from public use because it was a communist symbol, that this attempt dates back to the first elections and that all the parties participating in those elections had that on their agenda; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know precisely whether the five-pointed star was specifically referred to, but I do know that after the multi-party elections, Serbian flags were flown in municipalities with a majority Serb population and that the national symbols were introduced. And as I stated, my municipality was the last one in Bosnia-Herzegovina in which the police changed insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, that's why I'm putting this question to you, because I notice that you said in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so you will agree with me that where there was a majority Croatian population, in Herceg-Bosna for example, this change took place earlier as it also did where Muslims were in the majority; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection I think that Muslims started wearing Green Berets with their national insignia on them even before the tri-colour was flown anywhere. Whether the Green Berets were part of the police or the army or some para-military unit, I don't know, but they turned up first and I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Where the Croatian population was in the majority, the checkerboard coat of arms appeared even before the golden lilies did, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I observed the checkerboard coat of arms in 1991, but I'm referring to my own municipality when I speak about the change of insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, as you mentioned all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I just wanted to know whether you had any knowledge and whether you were aware that all over Bosnia-Herzegovina insignia were changed?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kljuc is a place of transit and I saw all sorts of things passing through.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let's move on. We'll just round off a topic that Mr. Krgovic almost completed with you, and it has to do with the termination of employment in the police. First of all, I'll just jog your memory and tell you that the labour law then in force envisioned that in all state administration bodies in the judiciary and in state-owned companies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Are you giving evidence, Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will reformulate my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if an employee failed to turn up for work for a certain number of days without justification, his employment would be terminated pursuant to the law, and this was the case not only in the police but in all state institutions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is under a certain number of days, could that be some more precise?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection I think it was five consecutive days without justification, but the witness can confirm if he can remember. Do you recall, witness, how many days it was?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not very sure about these legal issues. I think it was three or five consecutive days, not counting Saturdays and Sundays, so if, for example, you failed to turn up on Thursday, you would also have to be absent on Monday and then you could be fired on Tuesday, but you legal men will know that better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So we can clarify that this refers to five working days?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is that clear? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So all that remains is to clarify what it means when we say pursuant to the law, by force of law. So you will agree that this was a case where the law applied automatically, it did not depend on the will of the chief or the head of the unit, this was something that had to apply automatically; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when something is mandatory under the law, I don't know what happened in the SUP in the case of these colleagues of mine because I know that some of them had their employment terminated because they did not respond to the call-up. Whether this automatic principle was used or whether it was because of their failure to turn up for work, I don't know what the actual reason was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm only referring to the principle, to the rule. It was not discretionary, it did not depend on the will of a supervisor or senior officer, the law would apply if this was the case; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, when it comes to the principle, but specifically, I don't know which of these two reasons obtained in our particular instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. And answering my colleague Mr. Krgovic's questions, you spoke about the establishment of a parallel Muslim municipality of Kljuc, as you termed it, and its bodies, so I will ask you whether you were aware that a Crisis Staff was also established within the scope of these bodies or organs? I'm referring to a Muslim Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Assembly stopped meeting and when the Serbian Crisis Staff was established, they established their own Crisis Staff and they established what they call the Muslim municipality of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the first session of the Crisis Staff in Kljuc municipality took place?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that it was on the day when the incidents you referred to occurred, the attacks and so on?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was when I saw that all the leading people in the municipality were there gathered in one place, and on the next day I learned that this was referred to as the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will now talk about the incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, which Crisis Staff are we actually referring to here? Was it the new Crisis Staff that the Muslims had set up after the Serb --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I understood the gentleman to be asking about the Crisis Staff established by the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which of the two Crisis Staffs came first, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which came first. I just know that both existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I started dealing with the attack on the patrol in which your deputy was killed. The purpose for which this patrol was sent out was to prevent a blockade of the roads used by workers to go to the Sipad furniture factory, or rather to unblock all the roads. Can you assist us with this briefly in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you misunderstood me, yesterday, there was a report that the Kljuc Sanski Most road had been blocked near Krasulje, and this report came from employees of the Sipad factory who had a facility in Pec, and they could not get through, so they reported to the policeman who was on duty that the road was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Were other factories and enterprises operating at the time, not just Sipad but others as well?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until that day, up to the time when we received this report, everything functioned normally. We had all those extra measures in place, but I received this news while I was working out the duty roster for the following day, and there had been no indications that anything like that would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you just explain to us what escort service means within the station? What does it deal with?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that police officers do when taking a person from one organ to another organ. For example, if a court remands someone in custody, then that person has to be escorted to the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And the services or patrols that had the duty of escorting convoys or special kinds of vehicles in traffic, that sort of movement implied a special kind of traffic regime, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't fully understand you, but I can guess what you are getting at. For example, this escort service that you asked me about is when one or two persons have to be escorted. The second sort of task that you mentioned is done by security. You have a vehicle cleaning the road going ahead and then you have a vehicle in the rear, I think that's what you were getting at. In war time when we had reserve officers on duty they were not so conversant with all these details so they confused the two kinds of service and they confused the terms used to refer to them. You can find the definitions for these. The first kind is called "sprovodjenje" and the second kind is called "obezbedjenje."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So the purpose of this second sort is to make sure that there is safe passage?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I think His Honour Judge Harhoff asked you something about the functioning of the communications system, and you explained to us how this functioned up to the time the war broke out, and then with my colleague Mr. Krgovic, you broached the topic of how it was after the war broke out. So let's round this off, do you remember how long the periods of power shortages were? What was the longest period without electricity during the war that you remember?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be precise. When the conflict broke out, we immediately started having power cuts it seems to me. I can't really say anything precisely, but back in 1991 [as interpreted] there were longer periods when we were without electricity than when there was electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I believe you were referring to 1992, I'm not sure whether that is what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did it happen in 1992 that you didn't have any electricity for a whole month?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably but I cannot say anything with any certainty. I do know, however, that we were frequently out of electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was it also aggravated by the shortage of fuels and gasoline which further exacerbated the situation?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem of fuel was always a pronounced one, but generally we got by rather well through the aid of SIP. However, we had to act economically at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions, and I'd like to thank the witness for answering my questions so far.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good evening, sir.

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a few questions which have arisen from some of the questions that have been put to you by my learned friends over the last couple of days. Firstly, you were asked if you recall about the appearance of the Red Berets in the municipality of Kljuc and it was put to you that there were some volunteers from Croatia there when the war broke out who were sporting camouflage military uniforms as well. I just want to clarify, sir, were -- what is your understanding of the situation, were there Red Berets in the municipality of Kljuc that were separate from these volunteers returning from Croatia or did they form one category?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they all belonged in the same category, because the volunteers from Croatia were soldiers returning home and when they got drunk, they would fire their weapons and cause disturbance. The Red Berets on the other hands were a separate unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked some questions by Mr. Krgovic and he showed you the statement by Omer Filipovic dated the 29th of May; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That was today.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So I am assuming by your answer, sir, that you don't know who, in fact, took that statement from him?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when you saw Mr. Filipovic for the last time, what was his state of health?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he got in the car, he appeared normal. He didn't display any injuries and he had arrived on foot from Pudin Han before entering the car. Since the car was turned in the opposite direction, I know that he waved to some people along the way, and I believe they were members of the Muslim TO force which had attacked the bus I discussed earlier the day before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, to avoid having to redact large portions of the record, when you are going to have a series of personal question, we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do we remain in open session at this point, Ms. Pidwell?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, for the moment, and then perhaps I'll -- I'm very mindful of it now, Your Honour, so I'll keep an eye out for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked also some questions about the so-called parallel defence, Territorial Defence in Kljuc at the time and that these were the people that were being brought in for interrogation in the days after the events on 27 May. Who decided after the interrogations which people were to be sent to Gradiska or Manjaca and which were to be released? Who in fact made that decision?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said yesterday, I think, as far as I know those who were considered to be more extreme than the rest were sent to Gradiska, that was the extent of information that the service had. By that time Manjaca had not been established. That decision was made by the inspectors who interrogated them. If you recall, I specified the four elements: One, that they were members of the TO; two, that they had weapons; three, that they smuggled weapons; and four, that they displayed extremist views. Those were the elements I was aware of. I don't know whether there were any more. Those involved in such matters should know better than I do. The inspectors who interrogated them made the call, they did the screening and decided who was to go to Gradiska and who was to be sent home.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: These inspectors that you are talking about, who did they report to?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably each followed their professional alliance. The crime prevention service from Kljuc reported to Kondic, and there were those who occasionally came from Banja Luka and since they were from the crime department service they probably reported to their chief Djuro Bulic. If they worked for the state security service they reported to their chief. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You were also asked questions about the police officers who were put on annual leave and then failed to return to work and were subsequently dismissed, by both counsel. If a Muslim police officer failed to sign the loyalty oath and refused to wear the new uniform with the new insignia, would he have been allowed to work?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would not have. He couldn't work with other insignia on his uniform. He was expected to display the insignia of the MUP of Republika Srpska. They were prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You were also asked some questions about the incident that took place at the school at Velagici and you told us that -- or I think it was read to you that the municipal judge was present to do an investigation and we know that that was Jovo Dimitric. Could you tell us, please, whether you know if Mr. Dimitric was a municipal judge or was he a military judge?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a judge of the basic municipal court. In 1992 he was appointed president of the basic court in Kljuc, although I don't know in what month. It was once the Muslim judges left, including Djemal Botojnic. It was then that Mr. Dimitric was appointed the president of the basic court in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is something in the transcript that is insufficiently clear about the role of this judge. Perhaps the Prosecutor could repeat her question about the role of Mr. Dimitric at that place since I don't want to testify. The fact is that there is a difference between the interpretation and the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, are you referring to line 20? Where it is said that the municipal judge was present?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Line 22, Your Honour. Page 62.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 66, line 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, the information from my colleague is that the interpretation was correct and my question was whether he knew whether Mr. Dimitric was a municipal judge or a military judge. I hadn't asked about his role. I'd asked whether he knew whether he was A or B, and I'm not going to be directed by Mr. Krgovic on which questions to ask in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Except, Ms. Pidwell, it seems to me it would be useful, at this juncture to clarify this since it appears not to be irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm happy to be directed by Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's a suggestion, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, we've clarified I think, that Mr. Dimitric was the municipal judge in the area and not the military judge. In the event of a crime being committed in the municipality of Kljuc, as the first step in the procedure of investigation would the military or municipal judge attend the scene?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you recall in Belgrade Mr. Dimitric acted as my counsel. He said that he was present the next day, that is to say, the day after the event occurred. He said that he was present there with Vinko Kondic. I don't know whether you understood him on that occasion when he was clarifying to me what school it was because I didn't know where it took place, at what school. It means that he wasn't there on the day of the event but the next day with Vinko Kondic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Who was the military judge in Kljuc at the time?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know that the military police had their own scene-of-crime officer for certain minor offences that fell under their authority. I believe there was a military judge in Banja Luka who covered the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if you are able to, sir, and please tell us if you are not, are you able to distinguish between the role of a military judge and a municipal judge at the point of an investigation of a crime, the first point, when it's first been committed and they are first on the scene?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must object. The thing creating the confusion is what I pointed out at the outset. I was directing my questions at the on-site investigation, not the investigation as a whole. I wasn't concerned with the investigation because with -- I was interested in an on-site investigation carried out immediately at the scene when reports are drawn up and that is what was misinterpreted, or mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It appears that we have to continue down this path. Let's not wander too far afield, but the answers themselves seem to raise more questions, but let's wrap it up, please. I wanted to go back to before Mr. Krgovic's intervention, the last question that counsel asked, in the context of the witness's answer immediately before that about the military having scenes of crimes officer for certain minor offences and I'm wondering whether, Ms. Pidwell, your question took that what appeared to be a distinction on board in formulating the question between the role of a military judge and a municipal judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be of assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, your question does indeed give rise to some difficulty of interpretation. What exactly do you mean when you are asking the witness if he can distinguish between the role of the military judge and a civilian judge at the point of investigation of a crime? Because at that point I would imagine that the investigations carried out by some investigators who arrive to the crime site and start investigating, so are you asking who stands behind those investigators who are arriving at the crime scene, and if that is your question, then put it more directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I apologise if I've caused this confusion. My question was directed to the on-site investigation and the first person on the scene. If that person is the military or the municipal judge, what their role is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know in connection with this incident, the military organs conducted the on-site investigation. In terms of all the technical work and that, and that also a civilian investigating judge from Kljuc was also present at the scene. Why? I don't know. It wasn't a military judge but our investigating judge, but there were also the military organs of the military police. After the on-site investigation it was established that the soldiers were the perpetrators and then criminal reports were filed against them. Probably there was an agreement between the civilian and military courts to engage this judge if they didn't have a military judge who was in the field. That's what I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I found that helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You say, Mr. Witness, that it was a municipal judge who was there with Mr. Kondic; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: On the day after the event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So then that means Mr. Kondic knew right away about the incident, as police chief he's supposed to know, and if he was there, there's no doubt about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that, but I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pidwell, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked some questions about the Nikola Mackic school and we know that you went there on one occasion and you told us that people were being beaten by civilians as they came to the school; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know when the witness mentioned this, that civilians were beating people who were there. When did he answer that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I too had that question, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that he prevented an attempt to maltreat these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Page 32, line 24, the witness said: "I did not receive such reports from members of the police, but I could see that citizens were attacking the Muslim citizens who were being brought in." And we are talking about the Nikola Mackic school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But there is no beating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's a fine point, Mr. Krgovic. Please continue, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: All right. Let's clarify that. When you said, "I could see that citizens were attacking the Muslim citizens who were being brought in," what did you see?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got before the building of Municipal Assembly where Muslim citizens were getting off the buses, I noticed a big group of Serbian citizens who were shouting, making noise, and trying to kick these people. Whether they really managed to kick someone I'm not sure, but they really created a din and I suppose that there would be further attacks; therefore, I fired shots in the air and dispersed the crowd and that was what I said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Earlier you said, sir, that this occurred outside the Nikola Mackic school. What is your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Nikola Mackic school and the building of the Municipal Assembly are 15 metres one from the other, so perhaps I said before the school or before the building of the Municipal Assembly. It was between the old high school across the road next to the Nikola Mackic school. It's about 15 metres to the door that is the entrance to the gym. And when I told you that I noticed one of my policeman, Hamdija Kumalic, in the gym, I noticed him, and when I wanted to go further, I was prevented by the White Eagles who had come from Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about your knowledge of the maltreatment of people in the police station or at the Nikola Mackic school. The people who were interrogating the Muslims at these two places, you've told us, were the state security and the interrogators from Banja Luka. To whom did they report officially?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, our investigators from the crime prevention service from our station were also there as well as employees of the state security, and for assistance members of the crime prevention service came from Banja Luka. They were also inspectors. Our men reported to the chief Kondic, the chief of the public security stations. And these others I see now to Djuro Bulic or to Chief Zupljanin. Now which one sent them over, that's something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You also were asked some questions about your knowledge of the police escorting buses to Manjaca camp. Who organised the transportation of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Object. I didn't raise this issue in my cross-examination. My cross-examination was directed to the transport of Manjaca -- prisoners from Sanica to Manjaca by foot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't Sanica but rather Sitnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, the questions that I'm reading are not specifically confined to that. But if my friend is happy to stipulate that he didn't ask any questions about the transportation from the SJB Kljuc to the Sitnica school, then I'll leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow why you're inviting him to stipulate, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, without the opportunity of going through the transcript line by line, I am happy to take his word that he didn't cover that issue, but I - on my very quick reading right now - I'm not prepared to do that without his affirmation that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would have thought, Ms. Pidwell, that before you formulated the question it was on the basis of an issue that was -- that you were certain that was put in cross-examination, not something that -- not, how shall I put it, a gap or a impression that you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It's the formulation of the questions in cross-examination which are causing the problem, Your Honours. The questions that I'm looking at are formulated broadly. "You do not have any direct knowledge about the way these people were transported or who escorted them; correct?" Now, that's not confined to which part of the journey. I'm trying to clarify that in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but if you have a look at my previous question, you will see exactly which trip I had in mind. I said from the police station in Sitnica, I said Sanica though which was mistaken, to Manjaca on foot. So please check the previous question. I pledge my word that I did not ask a single question in connection with this particular transport.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honours' hands whether I proceed or whether I leave that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Having regard to Mr. Krgovic's declaration, shouldn't you leave it and move on?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Finally, sir, you were asked some questions about the electricity shortages from -- in cross-examination, and I just want to show you a document, it's P969, tab 37. Do you recognise the document that you can see on the left-hand side of your screen, and I think you have the hard version in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the report of the duty service.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if I can direct you to page 0629-3925. Page 248 in e-court. If we could just, sorry, look at the previous page to look at the date, are you able to see the date down the -- in the bottom paragraph there, sir, in the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3924, is that the one I should look at, or 3925?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: 3924, it's the start of the entry on it on a particular day, if you could read the date for us?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hand-over of duty, Vejin Marinko duty officer for the 30th of May, 1992, between 00 until 8 a.m. in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Turn to the next page. And do you see there at the conclusion of that entry just above the signature, could you read the last sentence starting around 440 hours?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Around 440 hours, I handed in a dispatch for the CSB Banja Luka in connection with regular reporting. There were no other news. Vejin handed it over. It was received by Mitar Dragic."

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when it says handed over a dispatch for regular reporting, what does that in fact mean?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether you remember when there were some questions with regard to reporting. I mentioned that there was an instruction about urgent, regular, and occasional reporting, and it had to do with reporting to the Security Services Centre and to the MUP. That was contained in the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: My question, sir, is does this mean that a report was sent?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So is it a fair assumption to expedite matters, where we see the words that a dispatch was submitted to Banja Luka, that it was in fact sent and if there was a malfunction that that would be noted in this book?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I would just have one question, a follow-up question to the Trial Chamber's question to assist with the issue of the military courts and civilian courts and their competency, if you might allow just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, as focused as possible, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether in the month of June in 1992 when the incidents in Velagici happened the military courts did not exist and did not function in the territory of Republika Srpska. It was only in July or August that they were established?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Was that a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question. Whether the witness is familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure of the date, but I heard that there was some military Judge Jovicinac [realtime transcript read in error "Milutinovic"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a correction, sorry, not Milutinovic, page 77, line, 3, but Jovicinac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can I ask to have 65 ter 2818 back on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I seem to have a problem myself. (redacted) this is that Official Note again I showed you awhile ago where you said reserve policemen Radojicic reports about someone who had fled on the day of the shooting in Velagici. What do you make of this Official Note? So obviously at the station one knew about the incident and now there is a report that someone fled from the scene where 79 people had been killed. What in your opinion as a policeman in that station is the purpose of this Official Note?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a note about something of security interest and probably this reserve policeman submitted it to the crime prevention service stating that the crime prevention service needed such information because they were questioning people or for the purpose that crime prevention service in the police should forward it to the military security organs. These were the two possible avenues along which this information may have been sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Were they questioning people about the incident?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: About the same incident, (redacted), we have heard that there was an investigation that when the investigative judge came at the scene, the evidence was removed, that means that 88 -- 79 bodies were removed with an engineering machine, I suppose something like a bulldozer, and with trucks probably, and buried somewhere in the forest. And we heard also in that investigative report that 12 men were charged with this crime, 11 conscripts and one 2nd lieutenant, and it was referred to as a bunch of drunken soldiers. With regard to the golden rules of criminology where Mr. Krgovic referred to, wouldn't you as a policeman ask how could it be done, the removal of the evidence so that the day after nothing could be found? Could that be done by 11 conscripts and a 2nd lieutenant, organise a bulldozer, organise trucks to remove 80 bodies and to hide them somewhere? What would your professional opinion be on that?

utterances.speaker: ST-218 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the logic imposes the conclusion that this group of people could not have done it. They had to have had logistic support from their units, from the army, and I suppose that they did it together with the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. We thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal. You are now released and the ushers will escort you from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We thank the interpreters, the stenographers, security staff, and the remainder of the support staff for their indulgence in enabling us to complete this witness's testimony this evening, and we now take the adjournment to resume in this courtroom at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 15th day of October, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.13 p.m.
